name: Journaling and mood
intro: Where writing is easy and mood trends are clear, and where the streak pressures and privacy leaks.

apps.title: How We Feel
apps.verdict: A rich emotion vocabulary with a two-axis scale genuinely helps people name what they are feeling. The free, no-subscription model sets it apart, and therapists actively recommend it to their clients.
apps.loved: A detailed emotion map split by energy and valence lets you describe your state with real precision.
apps.weak: The friend-sharing and sync features are unreliable, and that is the app's core social function.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to understand their emotions better without paying a subscription

quotes.text: I was recommended this app by my therapist and I couldn't be happier. The range of emotions and their categorization is so helpful for identifying my feelings. It's helped me learn things about myself I never knew. 10/10 recommend, especially if you deal with mental health.

please fix the sharing with friends, thats a huge reason i use the app and i just dont even want to open it since its been bugged so long. i dont ever see when my friends update and they do it daily and share with me i know for a fact.
I like this app because it makes it easy and quick to check in and track your emotions easily. You can see patterns and form coping skills with this app too.

apps.title: Daylio Journal - Mood Tracker
apps.verdict: Daylio is the best icon-based mood tracker in its category: pick activity icons and a mood level, get clear analytics over months. The downside is that after an ownership change, promotional clutter appeared in the interface and some users lost voice recordings.
apps.loved: Fully customizable activity and mood icons plus retrospective charts let you spot life patterns you would never notice otherwise.
apps.weak: Since the company was sold, the app has pushed intrusive promotional content, and some users permanently lost voice recordings with no way to recover them.
apps.whoFor: Those who find writing difficult but want to see patterns in their mood and activities

quotes.text: Just found out after 1 month of daily tracking, that I CANNOT SEE MY DATA. My own records are locked behind a paywall. I was using this data for MEDICAL TRACKING and foolishly trusted Daylio to hold onto it.

Daylio Randomly decided to delete all my voice recordings for the past 237 days. DO NOT DOWNLOAD THIS APP. I have been a loyal user since 2022 and I regret it. Personally memory with my grandma are gone I suffer from memory loss and this was the app I used to remember things and now that's gone.

apps.title: Good Things gratitude journal
apps.verdict: A lean gratitude journal with a well-calibrated structure: three items a day, a daily quote, and a PDF summary for any period. Reminders occasionally fail and the PDF export is sometimes incomplete.
apps.loved: The three-point format is small enough to do every evening and specific enough to actually work.
apps.weak: No streak counter and no way to jump back to a past entry without scrolling through a long list.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to build positive thinking habits without much effort

apps.title: eMoods Bipolar Mood Tracker
apps.verdict: eMoods is built specifically for people with bipolar disorder: it tracks episodes, medications, sleep, and mood in a single daily report that is easy to show a psychiatrist. The interface is neutral and does not overwhelm on bad days. The weak points are unreliable cross-device sync and an export that requires technical know-how.
apps.loved: A specialized psychiatrist report that shows weeks and months at a glance.
apps.weak: Only four severity levels (none, mild, moderate, severe) which is not enough to describe the full range of states accurately.
apps.whoFor: People with bipolar disorder who work with a psychiatrist

apps.title: Day One: Daily Journal & Diary
apps.verdict: Day One is the most mature journal in its category: multiple journals, search across years of entries, reliable export, rich formatting, and photos. The product is not declining technically but in trust. Aggressive monetization of AI features in the Gold tier and persistent upgrade prompts frustrate loyal paying users.
apps.loved: Search across the entire entry history with attached photos going back 8-plus years works flawlessly and turns the journal into a personal knowledge base.
apps.weak: Constant pop-ups pushing the Gold upgrade annoy even Silver subscribers and destroy the feeling of a private space.
apps.whoFor: Serious journalers and people who have kept a diary for years and value reliable export

quotes.text: I absolutely love this app! I've been using it daily for over four years and I have referred to it often with the search function to answer questions that come up. Because I attach photos to most entries, I can quickly come up with pictures of important events. The search function is invaluable.

I love this app and use it all the time. Moreover I've used it for 8+ years so the ability to search through journal entries, upload photos, and create various journals for different things has been great for organizing my introspective practices.

apps.title: Prompted Journal - Shadow Work
apps.verdict: Prompted Journal wins on prompt variety and the absence of ads: users come back because every day brings a fresh question, not the same "what are you grateful for." The weak spots are technical issues when editing past entries and a limited number of free prompts.
apps.loved: A library of 200 preset questions with the option to add your own eliminates the "I don't know what to write about" block even for people who dislike journaling.
apps.weak: When the free prompts run out, the flow stops abruptly, and without new questions the app loses its main value.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a reflection practice but need an external question as a starting point

quotes.text: I've been looking for a journaling app that has prompts but not the same prompt over and over again. I can only come up with so many things I'm grateful for lol. This has a lot of good prompts, preloaded with 200 and you can add more, and I do like the idea of getting to compare my old answers to my new ones.
I really love this app. When I'm having a hard time, I go to this app and write in this journal. The questions in this app are deeply thought about. Just a really really great app to unwind.

apps.title: Untold - Voice Journal
apps.verdict: A voice journal with surprisingly deep AI analysis: people note gaining insights about themselves faster than they did in years of therapy. Transcription occasionally freezes and notifications can duplicate.
apps.loved: The AI detects behavioral patterns in voice recordings and asks precise follow-up questions.
apps.weak: Audio transcription sometimes stalls for several days, breaking the journaling rhythm.
apps.whoFor: Those who find it easier to speak than to write and want to better understand themselves

apps.title: Emotion Tracker: Moodistory
apps.verdict: Moodistory keeps users coming back for years through its simple check-in, color mood scale, and the ability to attach photos to memories. The limitation is not the product itself but a fairly narrow emotion palette that does not capture nuanced states.
apps.loved: A color mood ribbon with photos turns the past year into a tangible emotional history.
apps.weak: The available emotions are limited and do not cover complex states like anxiety or mixed feelings.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a simple visual picture of their mood month by month

apps.title: Diary with Lock: Diary Journal
apps.verdict: A simple password-protected diary with theme customization and free access to most features. The audience is mostly teenagers who are fine with the low barrier to entry.
apps.loved: A lock that engages when leaving the app plus flexible theme customization without needing to pay.
apps.weak: No mood chart, no writing prompts, and no analytics. It is a plain notepad, not a reflection tool.
apps.whoFor: Teenagers who want a personal diary with a password

apps.title: Bears Gratitude
apps.verdict: Bears Gratitude wins on illustration quality and removing friction from journaling: a short entry plus a bear illustration matching the mood. Long-term users (3 years) note stability and the value of a one-time purchase, which is rare in this market.
apps.loved: The bear illustrations for each entry make returning to the diary an aesthetically pleasing and cozy ritual.
apps.weak: Navigation through entries is swipe-only, which is awkward when you want to quickly find something from the past.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to briefly record gratitude and good moments from the day

apps.title: Mirror: Mental Health Journal
apps.verdict: A newer app with AI feedback on entries, audio and video support, and a variety of prompts. Users appreciate the accessibility and prompts, but the AI still produces surface-level summaries rather than deep analysis.
apps.loved: Writing prompts that help you get started when you do not know what you are feeling.
apps.weak: You cannot edit a saved entry, and AI summaries take hours and amount to a paraphrase.
apps.whoFor: Those who are just starting to journal and want gentle prompts for reflection

apps.title: Diarium Journal: Private Diary
apps.verdict: A reliable photo diary with excellent search and a monthly calendar view, with stable sync. The main product flaw: photos can only be inserted at the end of an entry, not inline.
apps.loved: A calendar cover with photo thumbnails for the month gives an instant visual overview of your life.
apps.weak: Photos cannot be placed at an arbitrary point in the text; they always appear as a separate block.
apps.whoFor: Visual chroniclers who want to remember life through photographs

apps.title: Bear - Markdown Notes
apps.verdict: Bear remains one of the best note-taking apps in the Apple ecosystem: fast, beautiful, with powerful tagging and clean markdown. As a diary it only works if users build the structure themselves, and data occasionally gets lost during updates.
apps.loved: Eight years of stable performance with a consistent experience across all Apple devices and quick sync without extra setup.
apps.weak: The absence of a traditional folder hierarchy and mandatory tag-based organization puts off users who think linearly.
apps.whoFor: Those who write notes and keep a journal in markdown and want a beautiful tool in the Apple ecosystem

apps.title: Being Me: Journal/Goals/Habits
apps.verdict: Being Me offers a structured approach to journaling: morning and evening prompts, habit tracking, goals. Many users stick with it daily for months. The weak spot is an interface that feels cluttered in places, and the mobile-only format limits those who want to write at length.
apps.loved: Ready-made morning and evening prompts make it easy to start even for those who have never kept a journal.
apps.weak: Mood analytics are thin: the app collects data but shows almost nothing in the way of patterns or trends.
apps.whoFor: Beginners who want to build a journaling habit with the help of structure

quotes.text: I love everything this app has to offer. It has journal prompts. It has morning and bedtime journaling prompts as well as freestyle journaling, as well as quotes to get you through the day and it's completely free.

apps.title: stoic. journal & mental health
apps.verdict: Stoic philosophy fits the daily reflection format well, and the free-writing space is valued by long-time users. Prompts repeat, AI feedback is shallow, and cross-device sync is unreliable.
apps.loved: The minimal design and the idea of writing without judgment help people regularly express their thoughts.
apps.weak: Prompts loop quickly and stop being surprising.
apps.whoFor: Those looking for a daily self-observation practice in the spirit of stoicism

quotes.text: I like the app. It does encourage me to be more diligent with my journaling. It would be nice if the prompts didn't repeat so often.

Okay, I've had this app for a little over 3 years. And it's incredible. I remember wanting to be able to write down what I was actually thinking/feeling, However, it has become some so much more than just a hobby or way to organize my thoughts. I use stoic to set intentions for my day and reflect each evening.

This helps me to stay on track with journaling and checking in with myself and how I feel. It makes it an easy task and gives me a win each time I complete an entry. It makes it feel attainable and then helps me feel better.

apps.title: 365 Gratitude Journal & Diary
apps.verdict: 365 Gratitude builds a gratitude practice through daily stories, prompts, and mini-tasks. Many users stick with it for a year or more and report a real shift in mindset. The main weakness is content that sometimes repeats and an interface that is small and hard to read on a phone.
apps.loved: A daily story and a specific reflection question make it easier to get into the right headspace than staring at a blank page.
apps.weak: Almost no mood pattern analytics: the app motivates but does not show how your state evolves over time.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to build a daily gratitude practice with ready-made content

apps.title: Moodfit: Mental Health Tools
apps.verdict: One of the few trackers that genuinely links mood to specific factors like sleep, physical activity, and thoughts, helping users see patterns rather than just logging data points.
apps.loved: Charts showing the connection between mood, sleep, and activity provide concrete feedback that is easy to discuss with a therapist.
apps.weak: Periodic connectivity issues make the app unavailable for days at a time and break ongoing streaks.
apps.whoFor: Those working with a therapist who want to systematically track how habits affect their emotional state

apps.title: Bipolar Mood Tracker°
apps.verdict: This tracker handles the task of logging mood patterns in bipolar disorder well, thanks to simple daily input and weekly visualization. The parameter set is limited and there is no emotion customization.
apps.loved: Simplicity that means the tracker actually gets used every day rather than abandoned after a week.
apps.weak: The state range is narrow: only a spectrum from depression to euphoria, with no irritability, anxiety, or mixed episodes.
apps.whoFor: People with bipolar disorder and their families who want to track dynamics before a doctor's visit

apps.title: Tochi - Mood Tracker Journal
apps.verdict: Tochi stands out with its "mood as story" concept organized into life chapters, making journaling feel more meaningful. The visual language of a hedgehog character and colored orbs encourages regular use, though moving basic features behind a paywall frustrates loyal users.
apps.loved: Organizing entries into life chapters turns chaotic emotions into a coherent personal narrative.
apps.weak: After recent updates, features that used to be free moved behind a subscription without any new capabilities being added.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to see their emotions as a story rather than just log entries

apps.title: My Wonderful Days Journal
apps.verdict: My Wonderful Days has worked as a simple daily diary for over ten years and keeps its audience through habit and a comfortable design. Key limitations: the mood indicator is incomplete (no sad emotions), the interface is dated, and data occasionally gets lost after crashes.
apps.loved: Users have kept a diary for years and value how low-friction it is: open it, write, close it, no extra steps.
apps.weak: The mood slider only covers a range from neutral to angry, ignoring the entire spectrum of sadness and anxiety.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a simple daily journal without extra features and do not need mood analysis

quotes.text: Been using this app since December of 2012 wanted to journal my being days in the military ended up still using it after I got out and now I can't see myself not using this app. It's easy to use and very affective.

apps.title: Diarly: Diary, Private Journal
apps.verdict: A functional cross-platform diary with Markdown support and iCloud sync that works reliably for most people. Sync conflicts when writing from multiple devices simultaneously, and onboarding does a poor job explaining the basics.
apps.loved: Markdown formatting and stable sync between iPhone and Mac without any extra configuration.
apps.weak: When writing on two devices back to back, sync conflicts and entries get mixed up.
apps.whoFor: Fans of clean text journaling in the Apple ecosystem

apps.title: Grid Diary - Journal, Planner
apps.verdict: Grid Diary offers a genuinely flexible grid format with good prompts and photo support, but cross-device sync has been broken for a long time and spoils the experience for paying users. Long-term users love the concept; newcomers stumble over technical issues.
apps.loved: A structured grid format with configurable prompts helps you write every day without facing a blank page.
apps.weak: Sync between the phone and other devices is unreliable and loses entries.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to ask themselves the same questions every day

apps.title: Bearable - Symptom Tracker
apps.verdict: Bearable excels as a symptom tracker for people with chronic conditions: flexible setup, correlations between parameters, and genuinely useful at doctor appointments. The main weakness is an overwhelming interface, a high entry barrier, and new updates that periodically break things that worked before.
apps.loved: The ability to trace the link between food, sleep, and how you feel, then show the doctor a real picture over a month.
apps.weak: Too many steps per entry: many users quit within a week from setup fatigue.
apps.whoFor: People with chronic illnesses who keep a medical diary for their doctor

quotes.text: I've been really enjoying Bearable! It's easy to track symptoms, moods, and health patterns throughout the day, which is exactly what I was looking for. The app is well organized, customizable, and helps me spot trends I might otherwise miss.

apps.title: Rosebud: AI Journal & Diary
apps.verdict: The AI conversation partner genuinely helps formulate thoughts and deepen reflection, but users with intensive use quickly hit message limits and response quality is inconsistent.
apps.loved: The conversational format helps you get thoughts out and structure them without fear of judgment.
apps.weak: The AI occasionally mixes up facts from past entries and tends toward excessively enthusiastic reactions to any event.
apps.whoFor: People who need an accessible conversation partner for reflection at any hour

apps.title: Reflection: AI Journal & Coach
apps.verdict: Reflection offers real value: structured prompts, voice input, and sync between iOS and web help build a habit. AI reflection is still limited to paraphrasing, and the app is still rough around the edges in terms of reliability.
apps.loved: Structured prompts and an AI coach help people who could never stick to a diary write every day.
apps.weak: Voice recordings sometimes disappear, and import from other apps has been broken for several months.
apps.whoFor: Those who want not just to record but to work through their thoughts with guiding questions

apps.title: DailyBean - simplest journal
apps.verdict: DailyBean is the most visually appealing minimalist mood tracker in this category: pick an emotion for the day, add a note, view analytics. The core works great, but an ad after every saved entry breaks the journaling rhythm.
apps.loved: Themed skins and the small animated bean make the daily mood check-in a genuinely pleasant ritual.
apps.weak: An ad after every saved entry destroys the feeling of a smooth, quiet journaling experience.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to log their mood simply and beautifully without many words

quotes.text: I've had this app for several months now and i have tried MANY apps like this but i always ended up deleting them after a few days. This one is the best by far, aesthetically pleasing, easy to use, has every feature i wished other apps had.

apps.title: Orca: Formerly Happyfeed Diary
apps.verdict: Orca (formerly Happyfeed) is a gratitude diary with photos and a social layer for small groups. The low barrier to entry and the daily three-good-moments ritual work. The app periodically loses entries, and switching to a new device often means losing your history.
apps.loved: Three good moments from the day plus a photo: a simple ritual that genuinely starts the habit of noticing good things.
apps.weak: You cannot edit an entry after saving it, and there is no search through past entries, so it is a diary you cannot go back to.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a simple daily gratitude ritual, ideally shared with people close to them

apps.title: Simple Diary - Daily Journal
apps.verdict: Simple Diary honestly delivers on its promise of simplicity: quick input, fingerprint lock, photos. Users return and stay for years, but losing entries during crashes with no proper backup is a serious flaw.
apps.loved: A minimal interface with no extra buttons lets you open the app and write in a few seconds.
apps.weak: Entries occasionally disappear with no way to recover them, and there is no real cross-device access.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to write every day without any extra setup

apps.title: Clarity: CBT Self Help Journal
apps.verdict: The CBT structure helps identify cognitive distortions, and therapists actively recommended the app to clients. After a redesign, features began conflicting with each other, the AI chat responds with platitudes, and it occasionally switches to the wrong language.
apps.loved: The step-by-step CBT thought breakdown gives real insights into your own patterns.
apps.weak: Being forced to choose a streak length before writing feels like pressure rather than support.
apps.whoFor: Those dealing with anxiety who want structured CBT self-help

quotes.text: Instead of actually giving me any actionable advice or skills. The cbt ai agent just parrots useless questions back to me. Way worse then using Gemini even though this is supposed to be specialized.

I think it's good. I like how the Chatbot isn't like other apps, it actually remembers and analyzes everything you say and asks helpful questions. However, I hate how it restarts your progress every week… It's Sunday at midnight now, everything I said to the bot has been erased.

I should emphasize that this is a supplemental tool for therapy, and quite effective too, using it during the trial period alone helped me with my thoughts and feelings about work life balance, which is then brought up effectively in my therapy sessions. 5/5 for app itself.
I was suggested this by a peer aiding me in my mental health journey. Being able to deconstruct my thoughts and reassess how I'm thinking and feeling is so helpful!

apps.title: Finch: Self-Care Pet
apps.verdict: Finch is more of a self-care Tamagotchi than a journal: you set goals and "feed" the bird with your achievements. The core mechanic works and keeps people going for years, but recent updates (promotional events, inventory bugs, removed features) are slowly dismantling what made it loved.
apps.loved: Daily quests and the pet growing alongside you provide the small dopamine push that helps many people not give up on their habits.
apps.weak: The developers are increasingly replacing content with paid events and promotional collaborations, while removing beloved old features without warning.
apps.whoFor: Those who need a game loop for motivation rather than a text diary

quotes.text: This is the most satisfying way I have found yet to identify less beneficial habits and work on building newer, healthier ones.
As someone who is bad at finding motivation for stuff, especially when it comes to gratitude, it's really motivating to make a digital bird happy.

Finch overall was a great way to get rid of bad habits and maintain a routine, although sometimes you can just forget about it. If that happens Finch does a great job asking you why you stopped using it and why you're using it again. Finch is very good at personalizing its 'daily tasks' based off of what you need.
So sick of the paid advertising for a stupid movie. Used to have a 660 day streak now my finch just reminds me that even an app for mental health will sell out to make more money.

i used to (and mostly still do) love this app but i wish they wouldn't have removed the shared goal micropets :( that feature really helped me to incentivize certain tasks and ive just been skipping a lot of them since that.

apps.title: Gratitude: Self-Care Journal
apps.verdict: A simple gratitude journal with good prompts and a vision board. Serious data loss for several users and complete silence from support badly undermine trust.
apps.loved: Themed challenges and the vision board keep users engaged with the practice every day.
apps.weak: A hard streak reset after missing one day works against the user rather than for them.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a short morning gratitude practice

quotes.text: This app shames you for missing one day! I had 107 days of journaling, got sick, missed 1 day and this app brought my streak down to day 0, as if all those other days of journaling were nothing!!! Don't like this app for that shaming feature!

Earlier this month, July 2025, this app lost all of my journal entries since 2023 because of some sort of update. Some data didn't disappear on one of my iPads but all seven months of 2025 are lost. Forever. Period. Don't know about you, but I use my entries to learn and remember and for writing my book.

This app has become an important part to the start of my day. It helps me to stay grounded and appreciative. There is so much going on with the outside world. I need ways to keep peace on the inside. I recommend this app to my clients. My only feedback is to get more varied prompts. It seems they repeat.
I love that this app allows me to reflect on the top three things that I'm grateful for each day. And I also like that I can set a reminder to do so right before bedtime.

apps.title: Journey - Diary, Journal
apps.verdict: Journey offers a rich set of formats: text, photos, voice, templates, and cloud sync. It suits those who want a life archive across all devices. Weak spots are navigation that is sometimes unclear and sync that occasionally loses entries.
apps.loved: Entries are accessible from any device and saved for years, giving the feeling of a genuine personal archive.
apps.weak: No mood analytics or pattern insights: the app stores your data but does not help you understand it.
apps.whoFor: Those who keep a detailed personal archive with photos and want access everywhere

quotes.text: Not used to Journaling never liked the fact others would read my thoughts. Wonderful thing a password is! Not sure how to make full use of app but will come in time. Very happy I chose this one.

apps.title: Clearful - Journal & Diary
apps.verdict: A thoughtful structure for different types of journals in one place genuinely helps build a writing practice, though some users lose account access after updates.
apps.loved: You can keep morning pages, a gratitude journal, and a weekly review in one app with different templates.
apps.weak: No way to organize entries into folders or by topic, which is inconvenient when running several parallel journals.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to combine several writing practices in one structured space

apps.title: Perspective, a mindful journal
apps.verdict: A polished diary with a weekly mood rating and an interests tracker that many people have used for years. Development is effectively frozen: no export, no Mac support, and the journal grows without limit and can take up several gigabytes.
apps.loved: A weekly mood snapshot and interest checkboxes give structure to reflection without extra work.
apps.weak: There is no data export at all; the diary accumulates locally and can balloon to 5 GB.
apps.whoFor: Disciplined journalers prepared to live with abandoned development in exchange for a comfortable interface

apps.title: Card Diary - Journal, Diary
apps.verdict: The card format suits those who want to see a day on one screen and quickly browse through the calendar. Tagging works, but formatting is not saved and support has been frozen for several years.
apps.loved: Minimalism without forced "therapy" features and powerful tag search for people with a large archive.
apps.weak: Formatting (bold, italic) is lost on save, and the app has not been updated in a long time.
apps.whoFor: Those who have kept a diary for years and want a simple chronicle without extra features

apps.title: 1 Second Everyday: Video Diary
apps.verdict: 1 Second Everyday delivers a unique video diary idea built from one-second daily clips, and for those who have kept at it for years it becomes a genuinely valuable life archive. Recent interface updates made navigation less intuitive, and a regression in export quality disappointed long-term users.
apps.loved: An annual video reel made from one second of each day gives a sense of a year lived that no other diary format can match.
apps.weak: The new interface is confusing, and high-resolution export has regressed: 60fps was removed for the already-paid Pro plan.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a video chronicle of their life rather than a text or mood diary

quotes.text: I've used this app for three years now. I really love the idea of documenting each day. It's heart warming to see the video at the end of the year.

apps.title: Moodnotes - Mood Tracker
apps.verdict: One of the few mood trackers with a real CBT mechanic: you identify a cognitive trap and challenge it. It works as a therapy supplement, but widgets have been broken for over a year and period progress is only visible in the paid version.
apps.loved: The step-by-step thought breakdown through cognitive traps helps where simply rating your mood does not.
apps.weak: Widgets have been broken for over a year; mood analytics for a given period is locked behind a paywall.
apps.whoFor: Those who have done or are doing CBT therapy and want to practice the techniques on their own

quotes.text: i think u guys should not make that overall average result only for premium. thats what i downloaded it for so i could see all at once how i was feeling over the last month or week and i cant do that without paying money.
I've lost so much documentation of my life from this app. YEARS-worth. Yes, it was set to sync. I'm going back to a medium I can rely on: pen and paper.

Even though I see a therapist and work on CBT and ACT techniques, it can be difficult to remember to use the techniques during every day life. With the app I can set a reminder to check in and see how I'm feeling and challenge unhelpful thoughts. Surprisingly, there have been times where the app actually helped me work through certain thoughts.

I've been using this app for over three years and highly recommended it to my clients (I'm a therapist). The overall selling points were the simplicity of the app, icons and gratitude list. Recently they changed the gratitude list to some worthless and unnecessary prompts. Making it less effective as a tool.

apps.title: Journal
apps.verdict: Apple's built-in app with solid ecosystem integration: photos, location, reminders out of the box, and no subscription. But the editor is rough: handwritten entries disappear, undo is broken, and multi-device sync is unreliable.
apps.loved: Being completely free with deep iPhone integration makes starting a journaling habit almost frictionless.
apps.weak: The editor is unstable: Apple Pencil entries disappear and cross-device sync loses data.
apps.whoFor: Apple users who want to start journaling without downloading anything extra

quotes.text: I like it bc it's been helping keep an eye on my mindset due to things I've been going through. Only didn't give five stars due to the glitch with the streaks. I do this daily and don't miss a beat, but it keeps resetting my streak for some reason. Quit aggravating actually.
It's like you're expressing your feelings to your self and I can write about private stuff without people listening or looking.

I came from DayOne Journal and this journal is so much nicer to use without all the in app purchases! I do, however, wish that time stamps, dates, and locations from photos are automatically added instead of using 'Entry Date' as a default. I also wish that, like DayOne, it has 'on this day' widgets.

apps.title: EMMO - 日记与笔记
apps.verdict: Cute personalized emoji moods and Face ID protection work well as a concept. Chronic data loss when switching phones and weak backup make the app unreliable for long-term journaling.
apps.loved: Creating your own emoji moods makes tracking feel alive and personal.
apps.weak: When moving to a new phone, entries disappear and cannot be recovered.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a visual and playful mood diary on a single device

quotes.text: its a good app to write down your feelings without anyone coming to snoop through it because it has a passcode or face ID for u to open the app. ive been using the app for two days now and i enjoy just blabbering about my day and how i feel. i have trouble expressing my emotions and i think this app helps.

вела 2 года, перешла на новый телефон, вошла в учетную запись и ничего, все пусто, я вела его из-за своих проблем с памятью и я буквально забываю свою жизнь, а это приложение очень помогало, а два года жизни, которые я фиксировала каждый день просто исчезли…

apps.title: Gratitude Plus – Journal
apps.verdict: The app honestly does one thing: it reminds you to write three gratitudes a day and shares them with a close circle. That is enough for people with depression and anxiety as a daily practice, but the product is still rough.
apps.loved: A bedtime reminder notification and the ability to share gratitudes with a circle of people.
apps.weak: The streak resets without warning, you cannot fill in a missed day, and the family plan works inconsistently.
apps.whoFor: Those building a morning or evening gratitude practice

quotes.text: This app doesn't keep your streak. It tells you that you can't post. But the next day you post. It makes you reset your streak. Should let you have some streak freezes.

Really helps you think about good things in your life. During the day I'm thinking about what I might post and it helps me realize all the positive things. I wish it would stop asking me to upgrade though. I'm happy with the basic version and don't need to spend money on it. Love that I can share.

apps.title: Diary, Journal, Notes - Diaro
apps.verdict: Diaro is a mature cross-platform diary with folders, tags, location, and voice input. It works well as a personal archive with organization. The app looks dated, develops slowly, and password locking is unreliable.
apps.loved: Folders and tags for organizing entries: the only way to really structure years of diary notes.
apps.weak: No mood tracking, analytics, or prompts at all: just a text repository with no feedback.
apps.whoFor: Those who have journaled for years and want a reliable cross-platform archive

apps.title: Emolog - Diary & Mood Tracker
apps.verdict: A lightweight emoji mood tracker with widgets that handles daily emotion logging well and lets you scroll through past entries, but the sparse free emoji set limits how precisely you can express yourself.
apps.loved: A seven-day mood display widget on the home screen makes patterns visible without opening the app.
apps.weak: The basic emoji set is too small for capturing nuanced moods, and the extended palette is locked behind a subscription.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to log their mood concisely through emoji without deep text analysis

apps.title: Daily Tracker Journal & Diary
apps.verdict: A flexible tracker with powerful customization and good data history, but export relies on Google OAuth and periodically breaks, and saving entries is unreliable.
apps.loved: Wide field customization and clear charts spanning years of observations.
apps.weak: Data export regularly stops working and entries occasionally disappear without warning.
apps.whoFor: Methodical habit and event trackers with a long time horizon

apps.title: Journal & Mood Tracker - Halo
apps.verdict: Halo lowers the barrier for people with ADHD and procrastination: prompts and the "moment" structure help you get started. Free-form writing is limited, and the AI companion restates what you wrote rather than deepening the reflection.
apps.loved: Prompts help people with executive dysfunction start writing without getting paralyzed by the blank page.
apps.weak: Free entries outside the "moment" do not support metadata: no weather, activity, or mood rating.
apps.whoFor: Those who have long wanted to journal but could not start without external structure

apps.title: Reflectly - Journal & AI Diary
apps.verdict: Reflectly offers a structured check-in through questions and mood tags, which is more approachable than a blank page for people who struggle to start writing. The main problems are unstable login that wipes two years of data and broken widgets for paying users.
apps.loved: Daily question prompts help those who do not know where to start and gently build a reflection habit.
apps.weak: Login breaks and locks out years of entries, and home screen widgets periodically stop working.
apps.whoFor: Those who need guiding questions rather than a blank page

quotes.text: This app has really helped me recognize my mental health patterns and become more self-aware. Admittedly I use it inconsistently but the daily check-ins & reading my old ones help me become more stable whenever I'm in an unstable time.
It would be good if there was a way we can share out account or updates/ Reflectly diary with our therapists. I love how I can journal each day and attach my moods to it.
Would be nice if notifications worked consistently and if you could schedule multiple notifications per day.

apps.title: 5 Minute Journal・Daily Diary
apps.verdict: The morning-and-evening format with fixed prompts builds a solid reflection habit, and the product has a loyal core with 7-9 years of use. A serious problem: entries disappear without warning during updates and support is slow to respond.
apps.loved: Splitting the day into a morning and evening session structures the day and makes reflection a predictable habit.
apps.weak: The mood tracker does not function properly, and prompts do not adapt to the user's schedule.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a short morning and evening positive reflection practice

quotes.text: I really enjoy the prompts this app uses, and I find it easier and more enjoyable to use daily than similar apps. But I'm not really sure why they even have an 'insights' feature when the presented data is completely meaningless. I would love to be able to successfully track my mood over time but the feature just doesn't work.

This used to be a fabulous app… But the latest update, now streaks are all messed up even with the last update, I lost about 1500 days and custom text I created were gone and not getting reminder in the morning.

Wasn't sure what to think of the new Eva feature at first, but now I can't start my day without her feedback and questions. Forces me to be more detailed and specific, and feel like I can start my day with more actionable items. Love!

Overall, this is an awesome app, and I plan on getting it back into my regular schedule. I love how the journaling sections are separated by morning and evening, as well as the organization of the prompts! Also, I love the challenges and quotes provided.

Another app that doesn't acknowledge that some people work at night. When you ask me questions about how my day went, and I've just got out of bed at 7:00 PM, it feels ridiculous. Good job and goodbye.

apps.title: Habit Tracker
apps.verdict: Habit Tracker is a clean and visual habit tracker with pleasant animations and widgets, but the six-habit limit on the free tier hurts the most basic use case. Mood tracking is there, but limited to one check-in per day, which feels thin.
apps.loved: Swiping to mark a habit done and the audio feedback give a satisfying sense of progress.
apps.weak: Only one mood entry per day and a hard cap on the number of habits make the app feel incomplete without the paid version.
apps.whoFor: Those who need a minimalist tracker for three or four key habits

quotes.text: This app is great for the most part - you can add up to 6 habits under the free version which is fine for the most part. I like that you can add a note for each completed habit and then see a page where all of the notes are. I also wish there was an option to track moods multiple times a day as someone who wants to track my mood swings throughout the day.

apps.title: My Diary - Journal with Lock
apps.verdict: Those who care about privacy appreciate the reliable lock and simple entry format. Data loss when switching devices and no support make the app risky for storing personal entries.
apps.loved: Face ID and PIN lock give confidence that entries stay private.
apps.weak: No default account or cloud backup, so switching to a new phone often means losing everything.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a simple private diary without extras

quotes.text: this diary/journal app is probably the best one i've downloaded. all of the amazing features are free (not all but a good amount) no ads, and obviously the lock feature is something that i haven't seen before! i love how you can add a number pin if your forgetful like me, or add touch id.
I got a new phone and when I redownloaded the app there is no option to log in. How do I access all my entries on my new phone???? Someone help.

apps.title: Notebook - Diary & Journal App
apps.verdict: A simple chronological diary with no clutter: entries group by day, there is search, voice input. The main and growing problem: banner ads now cover the text.
apps.loved: Multiple entries from the same day are gathered on one page, like in a paper diary.
apps.weak: Ads cover all the text when the entry opens, and there is no way to categorize notes.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a minimalist diary with no account or cloud

apps.title: 2026 Planner & Agenda - Floret
apps.verdict: Floret shines as a visual planner: beautiful themes, well-structured day view, responsive support. As a diary it is secondary and offers no reflection or mood features, and the number of free event slots is critically low without a subscription.
apps.loved: The visual polish and well-thought-out visual hierarchy make it easy to stay in the system and return to the planner every day.
apps.weak: A limit of two or three events without paying makes the free version a decorative showcase rather than a working tool.
apps.whoFor: Those who want an attractive daily planner and are willing to pay for full access

apps.title: My Diary With Lock
apps.verdict: A simple private diary with a lock and offline mode that covers the basic need: writing without fear that someone will read it. Photos freeze and customization is minimal.
apps.loved: Users value the password lock and offline operation as their main source of psychological safety.
apps.weak: Almost no customization: one cover, no stickers, very few design options.
apps.whoFor: Teenagers and those for whom privacy matters more than features

apps.title: Stress Monitor - Moodpress
apps.verdict: Moodpress works well alongside an Apple Watch and draws users in with its visual design, but without the watch, half the features become useless. The diary component is basic; the focus is on tracking physical metrics, not emotions.
apps.loved: The bright design with animations and Apple Watch integration turn the daily check-in into a small ritual.
apps.weak: Without an Apple Watch, almost everything related to stress and activity tracking stops working.
apps.whoFor: Apple Watch owners who want to see mood alongside physical metrics

apps.title: Planner & Journal - Zinnia
apps.verdict: Zinnia is a digital scrapbook planner with broad creative options: stickers, templates, Apple Pencil, various covers. As a journaling tool it is weak due to an unstable editor and aggressive moving of basic assets behind a paywall.
apps.loved: A rich template library and Apple Pencil support turn journaling into a creative activity for those who like to decorate their pages.
apps.weak: The editor occasionally deletes written text on exit, and most visual elements require a subscription.
apps.whoFor: Creative people who want a digital scrapbook rather than just a place for text

apps.title: My Daily Diary ‎
apps.verdict: A functional diary with a print feature and a comfortable interface, but the story of previously free entries being suddenly locked behind a paywall severely damages user trust.
apps.loved: The print feature and the ability to keep daily work notes in a structured format.
apps.weak: No keyword search and sync between iPad and iPhone is unreliable.
apps.whoFor: Adult users who keep a regular diary and occasionally want to print it

apps.title: Daily Journal: Diary with Lock
apps.verdict: A simple diary with a lock, photos, and stickers aimed at teenagers. It works as a personal space for entries, but has no depth: no mood analytics, no smart prompts, and the format does not grow with the user.
apps.loved: PIN and Face ID built into the app give the feeling that it is genuinely personal.
apps.weak: No processing of what is written: just a text repository with no trends, patterns, or feedback.
apps.whoFor: Teenagers who need a protected personal diary

apps.title: Diary With Password
apps.verdict: An ultra-minimalist password-protected notepad that appeals to those who want to write without distractions. The single fatal product flaw: no password recovery and no cloud backup, so users lose years of entries.
apps.loved: No ads at all and the simplest possible interface let you focus entirely on writing.
apps.weak: There is no password recovery, and forgetting your PIN destroys the entire entry history.
apps.whoFor: Those who want the simplest possible diary with a lock and accept the risk of data loss

quotes.text: My texting can't keep up with my mind. I had recording my entries but I don't see that as an option since I made an entry today. Is there a reason for this? This really sucks.

This app is so useless! I forgot my pin ,I tried all pins I use but it won't open!…no forgot password option…I deleted the app maybe I'd be able to have access to my stuffs!!! Can't believe everything is gone!! I kept vital information about my life since 2021!! Only for it to be gone in a wink!!

I love this app for what it is but once I forgot my password to get in because it's been a while and there's literally nothing you can do to get back in if you don't know it. If you guess too many times it just locks you out. I can't believe there's no feature to ask you a secret question or to send an email.

I loveeeee love love this app but I can't remember my password and I really don't want to lose all my previous journal entries the only reason I gave three stars is there's no option to recover your password.

apps.title: Weekly Planner - Diary, Notes
apps.verdict: Before a recent update this was one of the best weekly planners with a convenient week overview. After the redesign, sync is broken, duplicates entries, and the free horizon is cut to one week.
apps.loved: Seeing the whole week on one screen and searching through past entries.
apps.weak: Cross-device sync requires a manual tap and creates duplicates; notes cannot be recovered after deletion.
apps.whoFor: Those who plan week by week rather than month by month and work from one device

apps.title: Waffle: Shared Journal
apps.verdict: The shared diary concept for couples or families is sound: the questions genuinely help people connect across distance. But an aggressive onboarding with a forced rating before first use and an abrupt move to a paid model undermine trust.
apps.loved: For long-distance couples, daily questions create a shared ritual and give a reason to talk about something real.
apps.weak: The number of journals directly affects the subscription price, so active users end up trapped: the more they used it, the more it costs to continue.
apps.whoFor: Couples or close people at a distance who want to keep a living conversation through questions

quotes.text: I absolutely love this app! My husband and I currently live 3k miles apart, this app has allowed us to connect on a different level is a safe place! Best thing we have done for our marriage!
Really good for getting to know your family and friends better plus you get fun and exiting questions!

I bought this app for our anniversary. At first it was full of great questions and we would get about three questions a day and we loved filling them out. About two weeks later we only get one question per day and when I try to add a new list of questions or something. It just says 'try later'.

apps.title: Grateful: A Gratitude Journal
apps.verdict: The simple gratitude diary works for those who have been in it for years, but a mass switch to a new subscription model cut longtime users off from their own entries.
apps.loved: A minimalist format with three questions a day does not overwhelm and builds a durable gratitude habit.
apps.weak: No grouping of entries by tag as a unified list, and prompt customization is only available in the paid version.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a simple daily gratitude ritual with no extra features

apps.title: Diary - Journal with password
apps.verdict: A simple and accessible diary with a PIN and font choices, suitable for basic daily writing. Critical issue: no cloud backup, so switching phones wipes all entries.
apps.loved: A simple PIN instead of a password and minimal screens on launch.
apps.weak: Entries are stored only locally with no backup; replacing your phone resets the entire diary.
apps.whoFor: Beginners in journaling who need the lowest possible barrier to entry

apps.title: Bujo - Bullet Journal&Planner
apps.verdict: Bujo takes the bullet journal aesthetic and makes it digital, but stability is lacking: entries disappear, sync lags, and the app periodically refuses to open.
apps.loved: Setup flexibility and multi-day tasks with automatic rollover appeal to bullet journal fans.
apps.weak: Data gets lost during crashes and after restoring from an iCloud backup.
apps.whoFor: Bullet journal fans willing to live with occasional glitches in exchange for a digital format

apps.title: Mood AI - Daily journal
apps.verdict: The visual mood bubble concept with multiple colors is original, and the AI feedback is appreciated by those who use it. Constant lag, freezes, and crashes make daily use miserable.
apps.loved: Visualizing mood as a colored bubble gives a vivid sense of the day's emotional state.
apps.weak: The app lags so badly that users give up journaling simply from waiting for the screen to load.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a beautiful visual mood tracker and can live with unstable performance

quotes.text: My favorite feature is the AI assistant because it really gives you advice catered to past knowledge you've put in entries and that specific recent entry. I have depression and anxiety and I struggle with identifying my emotions.

I love all the features of this app so much, especially the design, the AI quotes and tips and the overall aesthetic. The only problem is it's extremely slow. It makes it difficult for me to actually want to deal with it every day.

I love the concept of the bubble being multiple colors, i wish it was more like a specific emotion, even simple ones that you can put in it, as your overall day can't be assumed right then and there unless you wait til the end of the day, which i struggle to remember and identify my own emotions by then.

apps.title: Momento: Private Journal Diary
apps.verdict: Momento was built on the unique idea of aggregating personal social media data into a diary, but most integrations have been broken and unsupported for years. It still works as a plain text journal without social feeds, but the feeling of an abandoned product makes it hard to trust as a life archive.
apps.loved: The idea of pulling posts from different social networks into a single memory feed was genuinely original.
apps.weak: Social media integrations have been broken for years, data export does not work, and the developer does not respond.
apps.whoFor: Those who keep a text diary and do not count on social media integrations

apps.title: Moodtrack Social Diary
apps.verdict: A social network for venting emotions that once worked well but has been without support for years: login breaks, comments do not send, and blocks do not work. The product survives on the inertia of its old audience.
apps.loved: An anonymous community where strangers support each other through difficult moments.
apps.weak: No data export, moderation does not function, and toxic users are only nominally blocked.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to vent anonymously and get a response from strangers

apps.title: Shmoody: Mood & Habit Tracker
apps.verdict: The idea is solid: a cat guru, habit tracker, and life wheel in one place. In practice, endless tutorial animations and an unfinished engine get in the way of reaching the actual tool.
apps.loved: Gamification with points and cat animations keeps users in the habit longer than they expected.
apps.weak: Onboarding is lengthy and cannot be skipped; the AI cat has not been updated since 2022, and you cannot attach photos.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a gamified self-improvement format and can forgive instability

apps.title: Vision Board Perfectly Happy
apps.verdict: Vision Board Perfectly Happy is closer to a goal visualization tool than a mood journal. The core vision board creation feature works unreliably, the affirmation audio feels mechanical, and the app has almost nothing to do with mood tracking or reflection.
apps.loved: Quick creation of a video vision board from personal photos directly on the phone, no computer needed.
apps.weak: No mood tracking and no reflection tools: it is an inspirational slideshow, not a self-knowledge instrument.
apps.whoFor: Those who believe in goal visualization and want a daily motivating video

apps.title: Penzu
apps.verdict: The web version of Penzu works decently and offers a feature that reminds you of past entries from the same date in previous years, but the mobile app has not been updated in a long time and consistently breaks during voice input and sync.
apps.loved: Annual reminders about entries from the same day in past years motivate you to come back to the diary.
apps.weak: Voice input reliably cuts out every few seconds, making it practically unusable.
apps.whoFor: Those who journal primarily through a browser and value the retrospective reminder feature

apps.title: Grid Diary Classic
apps.verdict: The classic version of the app with a grid diary format that developers have effectively abandoned in favor of Grid Diary 2. Export is blocked, previously purchased features disappear, and the app crashes on launch.
apps.loved: The grid structure with editable questions helped turn writing into a habit without unnecessary decoration.
apps.weak: The product is frozen: features degrade and data cannot be exported without moving to the new app.
apps.whoFor: Nobody; the app is effectively dead

apps.title: Daily Planner & To Do List
apps.verdict: A beautiful digital planner with a large template selection that is almost entirely locked behind a paywall. Three pages per journal for free, $40 per month or $100 lifetime with no way to keep your data after the subscription ends.
apps.loved: A rich selection of ready-made planner templates with customizable colors and covers.
apps.weak: Data disappears when the subscription ends, and the free mode is capped at three pages per journal.
apps.whoFor: Those who want an attractive digital planner and are prepared to pay monthly

apps.title: Mininote - Cute note and diary
apps.verdict: Cute aesthetics and stickers attract a young audience. Data loss, freezes, and forced ads to unlock features make the product unreliable even as casual entertainment.
apps.loved: Decorative pages with stickers and backgrounds make for a visually pleasant diary.
apps.weak: Data disappears without warning and login between devices is unreliable.
apps.whoFor: Children and teenagers who want a pretty diary and do not plan to store entries long-term

apps.title: MyNetDiary Carb Genius - Keto
apps.verdict: This is a keto diet food tracker, not a mood diary. It has almost nothing to do with the journaling or mood-tracking category: no thought entries, no emotion tracking, no reflection. It works adequately as a carb counter, but the advertised analytics features require a subscription.
apps.loved: Convenient food search and a clear macro counter for the keto protocol.
apps.weak: No diary or mood tracking features whatsoever: it is simply a food log.
apps.whoFor: Keto followers who need a carb counter

apps.title: Diary - Private Note With Lock
apps.verdict: Diary - Private Note is visually attractive, but the key advertised feature, the password lock, is behind a paywall, which misleads users. You cannot scroll back through a long entry, which is a fundamental usability failure for a diary.
apps.loved: A visually appealing notebook-page design creates the mood of a real diary.
apps.weak: A long entry cannot be scrolled and re-read from the beginning; text goes off-screen with no way to return.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a beautiful virtual diary and are willing to pay for basic features upfront

apps.title: One Second: Daily Movie Diary
apps.verdict: The one-second-a-day concept is compelling, but the feature for compiling a final video breaks precisely when it is needed most. Users consistently lose an entire year of memories.
apps.loved: The simplicity of recording one moment a day builds the habit effortlessly.
apps.weak: Compiling the final video regularly fails or freezes, making the app's main value unreachable.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a lightweight video diary without worrying about the final edit

apps.title: Secret Diary With Lock
apps.verdict: A locked diary where the free user can create only 3 entries, after which every action is interrupted by an ad or a subscription prompt. The core function is blocked too early for the app to be genuinely useful.
apps.loved: Simple password protection with font options appeals to those who manage to get into the editor.
apps.weak: A 3-entry limit makes the app useless as a diary: reflection requires regularity, not a single session.
apps.whoFor: Nobody; the limitations kill the habit before it can form

apps.title: Confide - Video Journal
apps.verdict: The video diary idea resonates with people who find it easier to talk than to write. But videos regularly disappear, the interface freezes during recording, and pricing is opaque to a degree that some users call deceptive.
apps.loved: Speaking aloud and then rewatching yourself a month later gives a sense of personal therapy without a middleman.
apps.weak: Video recordings vanish after updates and support does not restore lost data, making the app a risky place to store memories.
apps.whoFor: Those who process emotions through speech rather than writing and want to see themselves over time

quotes.text: This app is truly amazing. It's helping me discover parts of myself that I never knew were there. It's like my own personal (Therapist). I highly recommend this app for anyone struggling with mental health.
I think too much. I get tangled in those thoughts, and then my whole life gets a little crazy. This is a perfect way to get my thoughts out of my head and untangle everything.

apps.title: Journal - Diary & Planner
apps.verdict: This is a decorative diary toy rather than a mood tool: users themselves call it a "game" and praise the stickers and colors. There are no features for mindful journaling here.
apps.loved: A bright and cozy interface with collages and stickers; it is simply pleasant to open.
apps.weak: No reflection tools at all: no templates, no mood labels, no reminders.
apps.whoFor: Children and teenagers who want a digital version of a pretty notebook

apps.title: Moleskine Journal
apps.verdict: After the rebrand from Journey to Journal, the app lost years of user data and key planner features, and trust in it as a repository for personal entries has been badly damaged.
apps.loved: A minimalist Moleskine-style design creates a pleasant notebook feel.
apps.weak: There is no way to browse a list of all past entries; navigation through the diary is only by calendar.
apps.whoFor: Those who value the Moleskine brand aesthetic and want a simple digital notebook

apps.title: Simple Daily Diary
apps.verdict: The interface is clean and extremely simple, but the payment gateway is broken: users pay for storage and still get blocked. No lock, no ability to back-date an entry.
apps.loved: A minimalist interface with no noise works for short travel notes.
apps.weak: No password protection and no way to add an entry for a past date.
apps.whoFor: Travelers who want a no-setup notepad, if the payment issue gets fixed

apps.title: Digital Planner – Task Journal
apps.verdict: Essentially a beautiful template viewer: without a subscription you get three covers, one template per section, and a handful of stickers. The pencil tool for handwritten notes is awkward because the toolbar covers a quarter of the page.
apps.loved: Visually beautiful planner templates with the option to decorate a spread with stickers.
apps.weak: Almost nothing works without a subscription, and handwritten input is uncomfortable due to the toolbar.
apps.whoFor: Those willing to pay for an aesthetic digital planner and not expecting a rich free version

apps.title: Secret Diary With Passcode
apps.verdict: The app has been around for a long time and retains its audience by inertia, but the systemic problem is clear: ads interrupt writing and erase text, and data disappears without warning. Writing here is not safe.
apps.loved: Users praise the simple interface and feminine design that invites personal journaling.
apps.weak: Ads insert themselves mid-entry and reset unsaved text, making the journaling process itself unreliable.
apps.whoFor: Those who want a free diary and accept the risk of losing entries

quotes.text: I've had this app since 2013! I use it faithfully. I opened it today, to write my daily entry and EVERYTHING is gone!!! Every single entry! How?!?! I'm so upset.
Terrible app. I switched phones and lost 5 years of my diary. I reached out but never received a response.

apps.title: Cub: Self Care Pet & Focus
apps.verdict: The idea of caring for a pet as motivation for habit tracking is appealing, but the app regularly loses progress, purchased items disappear, and without a subscription functionality is nearly zero.
apps.loved: The virtual panda pet creates an emotional attachment and motivates returning every day.
apps.weak: Progress and purchased room items periodically reset without warning, devaluing accumulated effort.
apps.whoFor: Teenagers who need gamified motivation for basic journaling habits

apps.title: Chronicle - A Personal Journal / Writing Diary
apps.verdict: Chronicle looks like an abandoned product: the last update was six years ago, the developer does not answer emails, and on recent iOS versions the app fails to open and destroys years of entries. Relying on it as a main diary is risky.
apps.loved: Users with a decade of history praise the simple and unobtrusive interface for honest personal journaling.
apps.weak: The app has not been updated for years and stops opening after iOS updates, destroying all entries.
apps.whoFor: Not recommended to anyone in its current state

apps.title: Diary-Journal with lock
apps.verdict: An attractive collage diary with stickers aimed at a very young audience. Entries occasionally vanish without explanation, which is a fundamental failure for a diary.
apps.loved: The collage editor with stickers and personal photos looks colorful and fun.
apps.weak: Entries disappear on reinstall or after a day change with no backup mechanism.
apps.whoFor: Children under 12 who want a pretty digital diary

apps.title: My Daily Diary - Mood Journal
apps.verdict: A children's visual diary with a lock that is advertised with drawing and stickers but delivers a plain text editor with heavy ads and unreliable saving.
apps.loved: The password and lock feature gives children a sense of privacy, which is valuable in itself.
apps.weak: Ads interrupt every screen transition and entries sometimes disappear on exit.
apps.whoFor: Young children for whom the idea of a locked personal diary is what matters

apps.title: My Super Secret Diary Notes
apps.verdict: There is a pleasant design and voice notes, but this is effectively a notepad with no lock: the core privacy feature is paid, and the editor offers nothing beyond standard text fields.
apps.loved: A pleasing visual style and low friction on first launch.
apps.weak: No journaling structure at all: no labels, no reminders, no history view by day.
apps.whoFor: Teenagers who want a pretty notepad with no depth

apps.title: Heartspring Journal
apps.verdict: The idea of a video diary for those who struggle to talk to people was genuinely valuable in the Talkbook version. The rebrand destroyed users' saved memories and moved video recording behind a paywall, leaving only the shell of the concept.
apps.loved: Seeing yourself in recordings from a month ago and noticing how your emotional state changed gave a real sense of reflection.
apps.weak: After the rebrand, video recording became a paid feature and all existing user recordings disappeared without warning and with no way to recover them.
apps.whoFor: Those who want to keep a video diary if they are willing to start from scratch and pay for the core feature

quotes.text: I loved the idea of talkbook (now called Heartspring). I have a hard time speaking with other people, so being able to journal my feelings and practice speech at the same time was super helpful. I loved that the video journaling was saved in app so I could reflect on it later on instead of taking up space on my phone.

I got this app back in Dec 2024. I loved being able to make little video diary entries. But they updated to 'Heartspring' and now you have to pay to record. You can type in your entry. But I think that loses the charm of it. Kinda lame now.

apps.title: Mood Tracker.
apps.verdict: The app aggressively requests a rating before the user has had a chance to explore it, which makes the entire rating meaningless and masks the product's real quality.
apps.loved: Basic mood logging and anxiety-relief elements appeal to those who actually make it to the content.
apps.weak: The rating prompt fires immediately after install, before the user can even finish onboarding.

apps.title: Diary with lock
apps.verdict: The app is effectively broken for its core function: an ad loop prevents creating a second entry, text does not save, and there is no backup. The lock exists, but the contents are inaccessible.
apps.loved: The lock interface appealed to those who found the app before the problem emerged.
apps.weak: No cloud backup; data is lost on reinstall.
apps.whoFor: No specific audience given the app's current state

apps.title: Diamond Diary Notes With Lock
apps.verdict: A diary positioned as lock-protected, but the lock is only available by subscription. Entries are not saved to the cloud and ads appear every few seconds.
apps.loved: The pink-and-diamond aesthetic appeals to the target audience.
apps.weak: The lock that users download it for requires a paid subscription, despite ads promising it for free.
apps.whoFor: Difficult to recommend to anyone in its current form

quotes.text: Bro my sister know my password and I want privacy and I wanted this to be my privacy but now I have to pay to get it locked the The only reason I got it is because I want to privacy and I saw a lock on the ads but I don't want this if I don't get a whole lot I need my privacy.

apps.title: Mood Balance:Self Care Tracker
apps.verdict: An anti-stress app with visual toys (slime, bubble wrap) that are almost all behind a paywall. Its real value for mood tracking or journaling is close to zero.
apps.loved: Tactile mini-games like bubble wrap give an immediate, if superficial, relief effect.
apps.weak: Almost no tools for journaling or mindful mood tracking.
apps.whoFor: Children and teenagers who want a quick stress-relief toy rather than a diary

apps.title: Memos - Digital Journal Diary
apps.verdict: Memos is trapped behind a paywall on launch: users cannot close the payment screen and get into the app, iCloud sync breaks with schema errors, and data disappears even for paying subscribers. The product in its current state is non-functional.
apps.loved: In theory the app offers a media diary with photos and templates, which draws users in from the store screenshots.
apps.weak: The paywall screen on first launch effectively blocks access to the app even for those who tap "continue without subscription."
apps.whoFor: Difficult to recommend to anyone in the current state

apps.title: Diamond Glitter Diary
apps.verdict: A basic diary with glitter design where written text disappears, there is no iCloud backup, and ads cut into any entry. Functionality does not go beyond a blank page with a password.
apps.loved: Users value the visual aesthetic and the ability to keep personal entries.
apps.weak: Text disappears on exit and there is no cloud saving.
apps.whoFor: Children for whom "sparkles" matters more than "saves"

apps.title: GraceNotes – Gratitude Journal
apps.verdict: GraceNotes is positioned as a gratitude journal, but the real user experience is a stream of forced ads that prevent reaching any journaling feature. Substantive reviews about diary tools are almost nonexistent.
apps.loved: The idea of a daily gratitude practice with a religious context finds an audience among people seeking spiritual reflection.
apps.weak: Forced ads after every action make keeping a diary impossible without the paid version.
apps.whoFor: Unclear audience due to a mismatch between positioning and the app's actual content

apps.title: Breeze: Start Self-Discovery
apps.verdict: Breeze is a dark pattern wrapped in a mental health app: aggressive ads, a quiz with paid results, and hidden recurring charges after canceling a subscription. There is almost no real product for journaling or mood tracking.
apps.loved: A few breathing exercise mini-games are described as nice by the handful of people who actually got into the app.
apps.weak: The business model is built on hidden recurring charges and making it impossible to cancel a subscription through standard App Store settings.
apps.whoFor: Nobody; the app's financial scheme makes it dangerous for users

apps.title: NE Mississippi Daily Journal
apps.verdict: This is a local newspaper news app from Mississippi and has nothing to do with journaling or mood tracking.
apps.loved: Readers value access to obituaries and local news.
apps.weak: Constant freezing when reading obituaries makes the app nearly unusable.
apps.whoFor: Residents of northeastern Mississippi

scenarios.name: Journaling between therapy sessions
scenarios.job: Log their state between sessions so they can come to the therapist with concrete data instead of a vague “things have been rough.”

scenarios.name: Writing down anxious thoughts
scenarios.job: Write down the situation causing the anxiety and their own thoughts, so as to come back to them at a calmer moment or discuss them with a professional.

scenarios.name: Building a morning routine
scenarios.job: Create a five-minute morning ritual that switches them from autopilot to awareness and sets the tone for the day.

scenarios.name: Hunting for patterns, not just writing
scenarios.job: Compare entries about mood, sleep, activities and events and notice the coincidences worth discussing later, without automatically taking them for causes.

scenarios.name: Keeping a serious multi-year journal
scenarios.job: Maintain a rich personal archive they can return to years later, search through, and never fear losing.
